content: Beta-alanine, also known as β-alanine, is the only naturally occurring beta amino acid. In beta amino acids, the amino group is located at the β-position, which is two carbon atoms away from the carboxylate group. The IUPAC name for beta-alanine is 3-aminopropionic acid. Unlike L-α-alanine, beta-alanine does not have a chiral center. It is not involved in the biosynthesis of major proteins or enzymes. Instead, beta-alanine is produced in the body through the breakdown of dihydrouracil and carnosine. It is a component of naturally occurring peptides such as carnosine and anserine, as well as pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), which is a key component of coenzyme A. Under normal physiological conditions, beta-alanine is metabolized into acetic acid. Beta-alanine serves as the rate-limiting precursor for carnosine synthesis, meaning that the availability of beta-alanine determines the levels of carnosine in the body. Supplementation with beta-alanine has been shown to increase intramuscular carnosine concentrations, reduce fatigue in athletes, and enhance total muscular work capacity. Studies typically involve supplementation protocols using multiple doses of 400 mg or 800 mg, administered at regular intervals over a period of 4 to 10 weeks. After 10 weeks of supplementation, the average increase in intramuscular carnosine content is approximately 80.1%, with a range of 18% to 205%. L-histidine, a component of carnosine, has a pKa of 6.1, making it a relatively weak buffer within the physiological pH range of muscle tissue. However, when L-histidine is bound to beta-alanine, the pKa increases to 6.83, making it a highly effective intramuscular buffer. This buffering capacity is particularly important in muscle fibers, where carnosine (beta-alanyl-L-histidine) constitutes 10-20% of the total buffering capacity in type I and type II muscle fibers. Carnosine is present in muscle tissue at concentrations of 17-25 mmol/kg (dry muscle weight). Beta-alanine supplementation, when provided in solution or as powder-filled gelatin capsules, can cause paraesthesia (a tingling sensation) when ingested in doses exceeding 10 mg per kilogram of body weight. The severity of paraesthesia varies between individuals. Some may experience mild symptoms at 10 mg/kg, while others report significant symptoms at 20 mg/kg and severe symptoms at 40 mg/kg. Interestingly, an equivalent dose of beta-alanine, when consumed as histidine-containing dipeptides (e.g., carnosine or anserine) in chicken broth extract, does not cause paraesthesia. This difference is likely due to the slower and more sustained absorption profile of beta-alanine when consumed in dipeptide form, as opposed to the rapid plasma concentration peaks observed with beta-alanine powder in gelatin capsules. In studies, beta-alanine plasma levels peaked within 30 to 45 minutes after ingestion and returned to baseline within 90 to 120 minutes. The occurrence of paraesthesia is not an indicator of beta-alanine’s efficacy. To avoid this side effect, studies have used lower doses of 400 mg or 800 mg per administration. Additionally, urinary excretion of beta-alanine increases with higher doses, with 0.60% (+/0.09), 1.50% (+/0.40), and 3.64% (+/0.47) of the administered doses of 10, 20, or 40 mg/kg body weight, respectively, being excreted in urine. This suggests that higher doses result in greater losses of beta-alanine through excretion. Beta-alanine also acts as an agonist for strychnine-sensitive inhibitory glycine receptors (GlyRs), although it is much weaker than glycine, the primary ligand for these receptors. The agonist activity hierarchy for GlyRs is as follows: glycine >> beta-alanine > taurine >> alanine, L-serine > proline. Despite its weaker activity, beta-alanine’s role as a physiological transmitter remains a topic of debate.
